title: One School’s Experience Is Not the Whole Story
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek, a school technology director and parent, responds to an NBC News investigation of YouTube use in schools by arguing that one school's failure should not become a verdict on classroom technology. He supports phone bans and closed laptops when devices add little, but holds that each tool should be judged by what students do with it, how it is designed and what protections surround it. Survey data he cites show most parents think school device use is about right while also wanting daily screen-time limits, so schools should welcome both support and criticism. He offers his Recalibration Framework, whose principle is that decisions begin with learning, not the tool, and which involves teachers, families and technology staff in documented, regularly reviewed decisions. Staffing is part of the problem, since a CoSN survey found 58 percent of technology leaders lack enough staff. He ends by asking reporters to examine schools that manage tools well and by noting that students still need practice judging sources on platforms like YouTube.
points: Judge each classroom technology by what students are doing, how it is designed and what protections surround it, instead of treating all devices like an unrestricted phone.
YouTube can be managed by blocking student search and comments while letting teachers share selected videos through the education player.
A repeatable review that starts with what students should learn, and sets documented decisions and review dates, keeps technology choices consistent and visible to parents.
Responsible oversight needs adequate technology staffing, meaningful vendor controls and transparent data practices, not only teacher vigilance.
Restricted school access can still teach students to evaluate online sources, a skill they will need once they leave those boundaries.
quotes: But one scenario should not become evidence that classroom technology itself is a mistake. The real question is when technology serves learning and what boundaries make that possible.
Schools should evaluate each tool according to what students are doing, how it is designed, and what protections surround it—not treat every classroom device like an unrestricted personal phone.
74 percent of public-school parents said their school’s use of computers and tablets was about right, while 75 percent wanted daily screen-time limits.
The framework’s central principle is simple: decisions should begin with learning, not with the tool.
Recalibration should become part of a school’s operating rhythm. Technology, student behavior, and instructional needs change, and a decision made during remote learning may no longer make sense.

Teachers should not have to manage every platform setting alone. Technology departments need adequate staffing, vendors should provide meaningful controls and transparent data practices, and families should know what tools are being used and why.
Finding a video is easy. Figuring out whether the person in it knows what they’re talking about takes judgment.
Show the failures, investigate them, and hold responsible people and companies accountable. But also show that schools have choices and that many are making thoughtful ones.
